steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a technical report on layered modal type theories. Explain the connection between S4 and meta-programming, why it is not enough for things like tactics that pattern match on code, what Moebius does and where it falls short, and then introduce the idea of layers and the plan of the report.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. S4 and meta-programming under Curry-Howard
2. Why S4 alone is not enough: tactics and pattern matching on code
3. Moebius: key ideas
4. Problems with Moebius
5. Our idea: layers
6. Plan of the report

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. S4 and meta-programming
- Curry-Howard: modal logic S4 corresponds to staged or meta-programming
- \square A read as code of type A, plus two axioms (T and 4)
- T: extract a term of A from its representation = run a meta-program, get a program evaluating to a value of A
- 4: macro inside a macro of a macro ... to arbitrary depth

2. Limits of S4
- convincing argument that S4 is a logical foundation for meta-programming, but facility hardly enough in practice
- tactics in proof assistants: refer to current goal, analyze its structure, apply strategies to fill it
- S4 only allows composition of meta-programs; no clear direction for case analyses of code structures

3. Moebius
- most recent breakthrough in this direction
- extends System F with modal types -> analysis / pattern matching on code
- (1) contextual types: generalize S4 setting, represent open code relative to a local context
- (2) levels: technicality, pattern matching on code must pattern match on code that again does pattern matching

4. Problems
- (1) preservation but no progress: no guarantee on covering of pattern matching on code; no matching case -> evaluation stuck
- (2) no normalization proof: unclear if well-typed programs terminate, even with covering fix
- fine for a programming language; type theory must be foundationally consistent

5. Layers
- this report: group of modal type theories based on layers
- stratified into layers (primarily two, possibly more), one common syntax for terms
- modalities distinguish terms from different layers
- simpler pattern matching on code + clear correspondence in semantics; seems to work around previously found limitations

6. Plan
- simplest layered modal type theory: meta-programming closed code
- then open code, then pattern matching
- dependent types: left to another technical report (size of development)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Under the Curry-Howard correspondence, earlier work found that the modal logic S4 corresponds to staged or meta-programming. In that setting, what basically characterizes meta-programming in S4 is reading \square A as the code of type A, together with the following two axioms:

In these two axioms, T says that we can extract a term of A from its representation. So T runs a meta-program and generates a program which evaluates to a value of A. Axiom 4, on the other hand, lets us use a macro inside of a macro of a macro of a macro … up to an arbitrary depth. Although this work made a convincing argument that S4 provides a logical foundation for meta-programming, what S4 provides is hardly enough compared to practice. In particular, tactics in proof assistants often refer to the current goal, analyze the structure of the goal and apply different strategies to fill it in. But S4 by itself only allows meta-programs to be composed. It does not give a clear direction on how to add support for case analyses of code structures, which we would usually expect from a reasonable tactic language in a proof assistant. The most recent breakthrough in this direction is due to a later paper. They propose Moebius, which extends System F with modal types so that it supports analysis or pattern matching on code. The main ideas of that work are:

- (1) contextual types, which generalize the S4 setting and support representing an open piece of code relative to a certain local context, and

- (2) levels, which in the end are a technicality forced by the fact that pattern matching on code must be able to pattern match on code that again does pattern matching.

This work has given ideas and shed light on how we should support pattern matching on code, but there are also problems:

- (1) Moebius has preservation, but it does not have progress. The main issue is that Moebius gives no guarantees on the covering of pattern matching on code. A pattern matching can find no matching case for a piece of code, and then the evaluation gets stuck.

- (2) Moebius does not have a normalization proof. It is hard to say if any well-typed program in Moebius terminates or not, even if the covering problem is fixed.

These shortcomings are usually not a big problem if Moebius is used as a programming language. But in type theory we have to be more careful, because our system must be foundationally consistent. In this technical report we develop another group of modal type theories, based on one simple idea of layers. The idea is that a modal type theory is stratified into layers (mainly into two but possibly more), but terms share one common syntax. The modalities are then responsible for telling apart terms from different layers. It turns out that layers are a powerful idea: they not only enable a simpler way to do pattern matching on code, but also have a clear correspondence in the semantics, which seems to work around the limitations found by previous work.

In this technical report we start with the simplest layered modal type theory, which can only be used to meta-program closed code. Then we work up to supporting open code, and after that pattern matching. We are also interested in scaling the whole setup to dependent types, but we leave that work to another technical report because of the size of the development.

steps.name: cited_draft
steps.text:
Under the Curry-Howard correspondence, [1] found that the modal logic S4 corresponds to staged or meta-programming. In that setting, what basically characterizes meta-programming in S4 is reading \square A as the code of type A, together with the following two axioms:

In these two axioms, T says that we can extract a term of A from its representation. So T runs a meta-program and generates a program which evaluates to a value of A. Axiom 4, on the other hand, lets us use a macro inside of a macro of a macro of a macro … up to an arbitrary depth. Although [1] made a convincing argument that S4 provides a logical foundation for meta-programming, what S4 provides is hardly enough compared to practice. In particular, tactics in proof assistants often refer to the current goal, analyze the structure of the goal and apply different strategies to fill it in. But S4 by itself only allows meta-programs to be composed. It does not give a clear direction on how to add support for case analyses of code structures, which we would usually expect from a reasonable tactic language in a proof assistant. The most recent breakthrough in this direction is due to [2]. They propose Moebius, which extends System F with modal types so that it supports analysis or pattern matching on code. The main ideas of that work are:

- (1) contextual types [3], which generalize [1] and support representing an open piece of code relative to a certain local context, and

- (2) levels, which in the end are a technicality forced by the fact that pattern matching on code must be able to pattern match on code that again does pattern matching.

This work has given ideas and shed light on how we should support pattern matching on code, but there are also problems:

- (1) Moebius has preservation, but it does not have progress. The main issue is that Moebius gives no guarantees on the covering of pattern matching on code. A pattern matching can find no matching case for a piece of code, and then the evaluation gets stuck.

- (2) Moebius does not have a normalization proof. It is hard to say if any well-typed program in Moebius terminates or not, even if the covering problem is fixed.

These shortcomings are usually not a big problem if Moebius is used as a programming language. But in type theory we have to be more careful, because our system must be foundationally consistent. In this technical report we develop another group of modal type theories, based on one simple idea of layers. The idea is that a modal type theory is stratified into layers (mainly into two but possibly more), but terms share one common syntax. The modalities are then responsible for telling apart terms from different layers. It turns out that layers are a powerful idea: they not only enable a simpler way to do pattern matching on code, but also have a clear correspondence in the semantics, which seems to work around the limitations found by [4].

In this technical report we start with the simplest layered modal type theory, which can only be used to meta-program closed code. Then we work up to supporting open code, and after that pattern matching. We are also interested in scaling the whole setup to dependent types, but we leave that work to another technical report because of the size of the development.

References:
[1] Davies and Pfenning (2001) Rowan Davies and Frank Pfenning. 2001. A modal analysis of staged computation. J. ACM 48, 3 (May 2001), 555–604. https://doi.org/10.1145/382780.382785
[2] Jang et al . (2022) Junyoung Jang, Samuel Gélineau, Stefan Monnier, and Brigitte Pientka. 2022. Moebius: Metaprogramming using Contextual Types – The stage where System F can pattern match on itself. Proc. ACM Program. Lang. (PACMPL) POPL (2022).
[3] Nanevski et al . (2008) Aleksandar Nanevski, Frank Pfenning, and Brigitte Pientka. 2008. Contextual modal type theory. ACM Transactions on Computational Logic 9, 3 (June 2008), 23:1–23:49. https://doi.org/10.1145/1352582.1352591
[4] Kavvos (2021) G. A. Kavvos. 2021. Intensionality, Intensional Recursion and the Gödel-Löb Axiom. FLAP 8, 8 (2021), 2287–2312. https://collegepublications.co.uk/ifcolog/?00050

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Under the Curry-Howard correspondence, [1] discovered that the modal logic S4 corresponds to staged or meta-programming. In their setting, what fundamentally characterizes meta-programming in S4 is the reading of \square A as the code of type A and the following two axioms:

In these two axioms, T means that we can extract a term of A from its representation. In other words, T runs a meta-program and generates a program which evaluates to a value of A. Axiom 4, on the other hand, allows the use of a macro inside of a macro of a macro of a macro … up to an arbitrary depth. Though [1] have made a convincing argument that S4 does provide a logical foundation for meta-programming, the facility provided by S4 is hardly enough compared to practice. In particular, tactics in proof assistants frequently refer to the current goal, analyze the structure of the goal and apply various strategies to fill it in. However, S4 in itself only allows composition of meta-programs, and does not provide a clear direction for how to add support for case analyses of code structures, as we would usually expect from a reasonable tactic language in a proof assistant. The most recent breakthrough in this direction is due to [2]. They propose Moebius, which extends System F with modal types so that it supports analysis or pattern matching on code. The crucial ideas of their work are:

- (1) contextual types due to [3], which generalize [1] and support representing an open piece of code relative to a certain local context, and

- (2) levels, which ultimately are a technicality forced by the fact that pattern matching on code must be able to pattern match on code that again does pattern matching.

Though this work has provided ideas and shed light on how we should support pattern matching on code, there are also problems:

- (1) Moebius, despite having preservation, does not have progress. The crucial issue is that Moebius does not provide guarantees on the covering of pattern matching on code. A pattern matching may find no matching case for a piece of code, in which case the evaluation gets stuck.

- (2) Moebius does not have a normalization proof. It is hard to say whether every well-typed program in Moebius terminates, even if the covering problem is fixed.

These shortcomings are usually not a big deal if Moebius is used as a programming language. In type theory, however, we have to be more cautious, as our system must be foundationally consistent. In this technical report, we develop another group of modal type theories based on one simple idea of layers: a modal type theory is stratified into layers (primarily into two but possibly more) while terms share one common syntax, and the modalities are responsible for distinguishing terms from different layers. It turns out that having layers is a powerful idea that not only enables a simpler way to do pattern matching on code, but also finds a clear correspondence in the semantics, which seems to work around the limitations found by [4].

In this technical report, we start with the simplest layered modal type theory, which can only be used to meta-program closed code. We then work our way up to support open code, and next pattern matching. We are also interested in scaling the whole setup to dependent types, but leave that work to another technical report due to the size of the development.

References:
[1] Davies and Pfenning (2001) Rowan Davies and Frank Pfenning. 2001. A modal analysis of staged computation. J. ACM 48, 3 (May 2001), 555–604. https://doi.org/10.1145/382780.382785
[2] Jang et al . (2022) Junyoung Jang, Samuel Gélineau, Stefan Monnier, and Brigitte Pientka. 2022. Moebius: Metaprogramming using Contextual Types – The stage where System F can pattern match on itself. Proc. ACM Program. Lang. (PACMPL) POPL (2022).
[3] Nanevski et al . (2008) Aleksandar Nanevski, Frank Pfenning, and Brigitte Pientka. 2008. Contextual modal type theory. ACM Transactions on Computational Logic 9, 3 (June 2008), 23:1–23:49. https://doi.org/10.1145/1352582.1352591
[4] Kavvos (2021) G. A. Kavvos. 2021. Intensionality, Intensional Recursion and the Gödel-Löb Axiom. FLAP 8, 8 (2021), 2287–2312. https://collegepublications.co.uk/ifcolog/?00050
